title: At the bazaar — prices, haggling, and one big trap
goal: Ask prices, haggle politely, pay — and avoid the two things that trip up nearly every newcomer: tomans versus rials, and the seller's تعارف.
bekal: ask about prices and amounts in three different ways
understand why the price the seller says is ten times smaller than the one on the banknote

dialogs.title: گفتگو — در بازارِ تجریش
dialogs.intro: Tajrish Bazaar in north Tehran. Budi stops at a stall selling spices and nuts.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Hello. How much is this saffron?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: سلام. یک گرم دویست هزار تومان.
lines.baca: salâm. yek geram devist hezâr tomân.
lines.id: Hello. Two hundred thousand tomans a gram.
lines.literal: hello. one gram two-hundred thousand toman.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: That's expensive! Don't you have anything cheaper?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: این بهترین زعفرانِ قائنات است. ولی برایِ شما صد و هشتاد.
lines.baca: in behtarin za'farân-e Ghâ'enât ast. vali barâye shomâ sad o hashtâd.
lines.id: This is the best Qa'enat saffron. But for you, a hundred and eighty.
lines.literal: this best saffron-of Qa'enat is. but for-of you hundred and eighty.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: How about a hundred and fifty?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: قابل نداره! صد و شصت، آخرش.
lines.baca: ghâbel nadâre! sad o shast, âkharesh.
lines.id: Oh, it's nothing, no need to pay! A hundred and sixty, final price.
lines.literal: worth not-has! hundred and sixty, end-its.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: باشد، قبول. پستهٔ تازه هم دارید؟
lines.baca: bâshad, ghabul. peste-ye tâze ham dârid?
lines.id: All right, deal. Do you have fresh pistachios too?
lines.literal: let-it-be, accepted. pistachio-of fresh also have-you?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: بله، پستهٔ کرمان. کیلویی سیصد و پنجاه هزار.
lines.baca: bale, peste-ye Kermân. kiluyi sisad o panjâh hezâr.
lines.id: Yes, Kerman pistachios. Three hundred and fifty thousand a kilo.
lines.literal: yes, pistachio-of Kerman. per-kilo three-hundred and fifty thousand.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: نیم کیلو لطفاً. و دو کیلو خرما.
lines.baca: nim kilu lotfan. va do kilu khormâ.
lines.id: Half a kilo, please. And two kilos of dates.
lines.literal: half kilo please. and two kilo date.

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: چشم. همه‌اش می‌شود پانصد و ده هزار تومان.
lines.baca: chashm. hame-ash mishavad pânsad o dah hezâr tomân.
lines.id: Sure thing. That comes to five hundred and ten thousand tomans.
lines.literal: eye. all-of-it becomes five-hundred and ten thousand toman.

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.text: بله، دستگاه اینجاست. رمزتان را بزنید.
lines.baca: bale, dastgâh injâst. ramzetân râ bezanid.
lines.id: Yes, the machine is here. Enter your PIN.

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.id: Thanks. Do you have a bag?

lines.speaker: فروشنده:
lines.id: Here you are. Enjoy your shopping!

notes: ⚠️ **Tomans versus rials (تومان / ریال) — the money trap that catches most newcomers.** Iran's official currency is the **rial**, and that is what is printed on the banknotes. But nobody quotes prices in rials. Everyone — sellers, drivers, waiters, cashiers — talks in **tomans**, and **one toman = ten rials**. If the seller says صد هزار تومان, the card machine will show ۱٬۰۰۰٬۰۰۰ ریال. Don't panic: add a zero and everything matches.

⚠️ **And there's a second layer: the word هزار is often dropped.** Since prices in Iran run into the hundreds of thousands, people in Tehran shorten them: صد و هشتاد in this dialogue means صد و هشتاد **هزار** تومان. A rule of thumb that always helps: **if a price sounds impossibly cheap, the هزار has been dropped.** If in doubt, ask: هزار تومان؟ — nobody will be offended.

⚠️⚠️ **The phrase قابل نداره is the most dangerous sentence in this book, and you must NOT believe it.** Literally "it's not worthy (of you)" — meaning "take it, it's free". The seller does **not** mean to give you anything for free. This is تعارف, a ritual of polite self-effacement that must be said and must be declined. Your reply: خواهش می‌کنم، چقدر تقدیم کنم؟ (*khâhesh mikonam, cheghadr taghdim konam?*, "how much may I offer you?"), or simply ask the price again. If you take the goods and walk off, you are stealing. The whole تعارف system is taken apart in unit 15.

**Both نیم and نصف mean "half", but they aren't interchangeable.** نیم goes before a measure: نیم کیلو ("half a kilo"), نیم ساعت ("half an hour"). نصف is for splitting something: نصفِ نان ("half the bread"), نصفِ پول ("half the money").

***Kârt mikeshid?*** **(کارت می‌کشید؟) literally means "do you pull a card?"** — from the motion of swiping it through the machine. Almost every stall in Iran takes local debit cards, but ⚠️ **international credit cards (Visa, Mastercard) don't work in Iran at all.** Bring cash or get a local tourist card before you go.

***Kharid mobârak!*** **(خرید مبارک) = "enjoy your purchase!"** What the seller says as you leave. مبارک appears in many congratulations: تولدت مبارک ("happy birthday"), عیدت مبارک ("happy holiday"), مبارک باشد ("may it bring blessings"). It's the same word as the *Mubarak* in "Eid Mubarak".

grammars.title: Three ways to ask the price
after: **The word چند** asks about countable numbers, **چقدر** about quantity or price in general. For prices, both are correct and equally common.
Spoken forms: چنده؟ (*chande?*), چقدره؟ (*cheghadre?*), قیمتش چنده؟ (*ghymatash chande?*). You'll hear these short forms far more often than the long ones.

grammars.title: Haggling without sounding rude
body: Haggling is normal in traditional bazaars (بازار), carpet shops, and street taxis — and **not** in supermarkets, shops with price tags, or restaurants. The key isn't being tough but being friendly: haggling in Iran is a conversation, not a fight.
after: ⚠️ **Don't haggle with a stern face or a pushy tone.** What works in Iran is a smile, praise for the goods, and a willingness to walk away. Saying فعلاً نه، ممنون as you slowly step off often gets you a new price before you reach the door.
**A reasonable opening offer is about 70-80 percent of the asking price**, not half. Offering too little is seen as rude, not clever.
If the seller says **قیمت مقطوع است** (*ghymat maghtu' ast*, "fixed price") or you see a printed price tag, stop — haggling doesn't apply there.

grammars.title: Weights, measures, and packaging
after: To order: **number + measure + item**. دو کیلو خرما، یک بسته چای، سه تا سیب، نیم کیلو پسته. The order is just like English "two kilos of dates", only without the "of".

sections.title: What's sold at an Iranian bazaar

blocks.text: Note two words that carry history: **سیب‌زمینی** ("potato") is literally "earth apple" (just like French *pomme de terre*), and **گوجه‌فرنگی** ("tomato") is literally "foreign plum" — tomatoes really did come from the Americas via Europe. The word فرنگی ("Frankish, European") also appears in توت‌فرنگی ("strawberry", literally "foreign mulberry").

blocks.title: Words you already know
items: *Bâzâr* **بازار** → "bazaar". *Peste* **پسته** → "pistachio". *Limu* **لیمو** → "lemon". *Nârenj* **نارنج** → "orange". *Ghand* **قند** ("sugar lump") → "candy". Trade words that traveled west from Persia along the old caravan routes — the ones you "learn" now you only need to recognize again.

⚠️ But watch out for words with several meanings: **شیر** (*shir*) means "milk" — and also "lion" and "tap". Context always separates them, but a sign saying شیر on a bathroom wall is not promising you milk. And **ماست** (*mâst*) is **yogurt**, a staple at every meal.

blocks.title: Six phrases for a whole shopping trip
items: "How much is this?" — این چقدر است؟
"Don't you have anything cheaper?" — ارزان‌تر ندارید؟
"How much is it altogether?" — همه‌اش چقدر شد؟
"Can I pay by card?" — کارت می‌کشید؟
"Do you have a bag?" — کیسه دارید؟ These six phrases cover all your shopping in Iran, and five of them work in restaurants and taxis too.
Asking the price per kilo: ____ چند؟
Asking for a discount: ____ بدهید لطفاً.
Asking for the total: همه‌اش چقدر ____؟
The seller says صد هزار تومان. How many rials is that? ____ ریال
Ten percent of صد هزار is ____
A hundred and fifty thousand, written in words: ____

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
